text:
The irresolution of Oswald's character, increased by his misfortunes, inclined him to fear every irrevocable course. In his uncertainty, he had not even dared to ask Corinne the secret of her name and her fate, and yet his love for her was gaining new strength every day; he never looked at her without emotion; in company, he could scarcely move away, even for an instant, from the place where she was sitting; she did not utter a word that he did not feel; she did not have an instant of sadness or gaiety whose reflection was not depicted on his own countenance. But, even as he admired, even as he loved Corinne, he remembered how ill such a woman accorded with the English way of life, how much she differed from his father's conception of the woman it would be fitting for him to marry; and what he said to Corinne bore the marks of the agitation and constraint that these reflections aroused in him.

Corinne was only too well aware of it; but it would have cost her so much to break with Lord Nelvil that she herself acquiesced in there being no decisive explanation between them; and as there was a certain lack of foresight in her character, she was happy with the present as it was, although it was impossible for her to know what would come of it.

She had withdrawn entirely from society to devote herself to her feelings for Oswald. But at last, wounded by his silence about their future, she resolved to accept an invitation to a ball where her presence was eagerly desired. Nothing is regarded with more indifference in Rome than withdrawing from society and reappearing in it by turns, as it suits one: it is the country where people concern themselves least with what elsewhere is called gossip; everyone does as he pleases without anyone inquiring into it, unless in others one encounters an obstacle to one's love or ambition. The Romans are no more concerned about the conduct of their compatriots than about that of the foreigners who come and go through their city, the meeting place of Europeans. When Lord Nelvil learned that Corinne was going to the ball, he felt vexed. For some time he had thought he saw in her a melancholy disposition that sympathized with his own; all at once she appeared to him keenly preoccupied with dancing, with that talent in which she excelled, and her imagination seemed animated by the prospect of a celebration. Corinne was not a frivolous person, but every day she felt herself more subjugated by her love for Oswald, and she wanted to try to weaken its force. She knew from experience that reflection and sacrifices have less power over passionate natures than distraction does, and she thought that reason consists not in triumphing over oneself according to the rules, but as best one can.

“I must,” she said to Lord Nelvil, who was reproaching her for this intention, “I must nevertheless find out whether there is no one but you left in the world who can fill my life, whether what pleased me formerly can no longer amuse me, and whether the feeling you inspire in me must absorb every other interest and every other thought.”—“So you wish to cease loving me?” Oswald replied.—“No,” Corinne answered; “but only in domestic life can it be sweet to feel oneself thus ruled by a single affection. For me, who need my talents, my wit, my imagination, to sustain the brilliance of the life I have adopted, it hurts me, and hurts me greatly, to love as I love you.”—“So you would not sacrifice to me,” Oswald said to her, “that homage, that glory?”—“What does it matter to you,” Corinne said, “to know whether I would sacrifice them to you! Since we are not destined for one another, you must not forever blight for me the kind of happiness with which I must content myself.” Lord Nelvil did not reply, because, in expressing his feeling, he would also have had to say what design that feeling inspired in him; and his heart did not yet know. He therefore remained silent, sighing, and followed Corinne to the ball, although it cost him a great deal to go there.

It was the first time since his misfortune that he had again seen a large gathering; and the tumult of a celebration produced in him such an impression of sadness that he remained for a long time in a room adjoining the ballroom, his head resting on his hand, without even seeking to watch Corinne dance. He listened to that dance music which, like all music, makes one dream, although it seems intended only for joy. The Count d’Erfeuil arrived, utterly delighted by a ball, a gathering, in short, by a numerous company that reminded him a little of France. “I have done all I could,” he said to Lord Nelvil, “to find some interest in those ruins about which there is so much talk in Rome; I see nothing beautiful in them: admiration for those fragments covered with brambles is a prejudice. I shall give my opinion of them when I return to Paris, for it is time that this enchantment with Italy should end. There is not a monument in Europe still standing whole today that is not worth more than those broken columns, those bas-reliefs blackened by time, which can be admired only by dint of erudition. A pleasure that must be purchased with so much study does not seem to me very keen in itself; for no one needs to grow pale over books in order to be enraptured by the spectacles of Paris.” Lord Nelvil made no reply. The Count d’Erfeuil questioned him again about the impression Rome had made on him. “In the midst of a ball,” Oswald said, “this is hardly the time to speak of it seriously, and you know that I do not know how to speak otherwise.”—“Very well,” the Count d’Erfeuil replied; “I am gayer than you, I admit it; but who knows whether I am not wiser? There is a great deal of philosophy, believe me, in my apparent lightness; life must be taken that way.”—“You may be right,” Oswald replied; “but it is by nature, and not through reflection, that you are so, and that is why your way of being suits no one but you.”

The Count d’Erfeuil heard Corinne's name mentioned in the ballroom, and he went in to find out what was happening. Lord Nelvil advanced as far as the door and saw the Prince of Amalfi, a Neapolitan of the handsomest appearance, asking Corinne to dance the Tarantella with him, a dance from Naples, full of grace and originality. Corinne's friends were asking her to do so as well. She accepted without waiting to be pressed, which greatly surprised the Count d’Erfeuil, accustomed as he was to the refusals with which it is customary to preface consent. But in Italy, that kind of affectation is unknown, and everyone quite simply believes that one pleases society more by readily doing what it desires. Corinne would have invented this natural manner had it not already been customary. The dress she had put on for the ball was elegant and light; her hair was gathered into a silk net in the Italian fashion, and her eyes expressed a keen pleasure that made her more alluring than ever. Oswald was troubled by it; he struggled against himself; he was indignant at being captivated by charms of which he ought to complain, since, far from thinking of pleasing him, it was almost in order to escape his sway that Corinne showed herself so ravishing. But who can resist the seductions of grace? Even were it disdainful, it would still be all-powerful; and that was assuredly not Corinne's disposition. She caught sight of Lord Nelvil, blushed, and, as she looked at him, her eyes held an enchanting tenderness.
